utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. Before I call for the appearances, the -- whereas the parties are aware as to why we didn't sit next week -- last week, I'm sorry, the -- before we begin today's proceedings, I wish to state publicly for the record that the -- last week the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel and support staff did have a site visit and the -- whereas it was obviously an expensive exercise, the inestimatable value of being able to see for ourselves, particularly those of us who are the triers of the facts, is something which will obviously resound to the benefit of the final judgement when we come to write it and we will be issuing formal letters of thanks to those concerned, but I would wish at this point to thank the Registry who would have facilitated this, the support staff, the interpreters, the security persons, and especially the authorities in Bosnia who ensured our safety during the six days that we were there. And of course the co-operation of counsel on both sides, and we are all agreed that it was a quite useful exercise, which as I said would be of ultimate benefit to all of us when we come to the end of this case. Yes, may I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Welcome back. I'm Tom Hannis, along with Jasmina Bosnjakovic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present in the court. He already signed a waiver and will not be in the court until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Before I continue, I see that according to the transcript I said at line 14 Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, of course I meant counsel on both sides. Thank you. Mr. Hannis, we are given to understand that there is a application which the OTP has to make first thing this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We filed a written application. The next witness is ST-215. I met with him for the first time on Friday, and for the first time in our contacts with him he indicated that he wished to have certain protective measures. So we filed a written motion on Friday indicating that he was seeking to have the protective measures of a pseudonym and voice -- and image distortion. What I proposed to do was because of the short notice is to have him come in in private session and he can answer Your Honours' questions about why he thinks he needs those measures. I said briefly in the motion his concerns, but I think it's better addressed with you particularly one-on-one with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we go into closed session, there is one housekeeping matter which -- just in the event that I forget it later. We have been -- I think everybody is aware of the problems with Courtroom II, and as a consequence we have been requested to move tomorrow's sitting to the afternoon instead of the morning. The Trial Chamber has decided that we have little choice in the matter. I only trust that this is -- that there is no inconvenience to counsel by this move. So you are on notice that when we take the adjournment today we will be resuming I believe in Courtroom I, thank you, at 2.15 tomorrow. Yes. So we go into closed session. Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I understand that there is a face distortion on the internet, but he's open to the public. Yes, he needs the screens, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the pseudonym sheet is admitted and marked as an exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. That will be Exhibit P1604 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if we put on the record that the witness looked at it and confirmed that the information is correct as far as his name and date of birth. We can do that I guess when we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Now the blinds can be opened. Mr. Witness, before I invite Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution to begin, there are a few more preliminary questions which I would put to you. The -- some of the matters have already been dealt with in the course of the preliminary examination that we would have had dealing with the application for protective measures. The first question I would ask you to confirm is that the pseudonym sheet which was handed to you by the Prosecution and which you've signed accurately states your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And could you tell us what your profession is or was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm reminded that we need to go into private session to deal with this. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously before this Tribunal or before any of the courts in any of the countries of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Prosecution has called you as a witness in this hearing and the procedure of the Tribunal is the side calling you will begin by asking you questions. Mr. Hannis, could you remind me as to how much time you've indicated you will spend with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Four hours, Your Honour, I believe is what we asked and been given. I hope to be a bit shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not more than two sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That would be roughly two hours and 40 minutes? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and perhaps even less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will probably not cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So you would have heard, sir, from what has just passed between the Bench and counsel that the total time that the examination -- questions by counsel would take is approximately a little less than six, six and a half hours. Now, the -- as I said, the Prosecution would begin, then counsel for Mr. Stanisic would have questions of you. Counsel for Mr. Zupljanin has indicated that he doesn't intend to cross-examine. Counsel for the Prosecution would then have a right to re-examine you, and then at that stage or indeed at any earlier stage the Bench may have questions for you. For technical reasons and also for the comfort of witnesses and counsel and everyone concerned, the sessions - and you heard Mr. Cvijetic use the word "sessions" - are of no more than 90 minutes in length, indeed they are more like an hour and 20 minutes. And the technical reasons the tapes used by which these recordings are memorialised have to be changed, and, as I said, it also allows for the comfort and convenience of everyone else. And we usually begin -- this is a morning sitting so we would sit from 9.00 in the morning until 1.45, but as I said between -- that is broken up into sessions to allow for the technical and other matters to which I have referred. Now for certain reasons, tomorrow afternoon -- because your testimony would not have been completed by the time we rise today at 1.45, we would be sitting in the afternoon. So we would sit from 2.15 in the afternoon until 7.00 p.m., but again the breaks would be similar. Now, notwithstanding those breaks to which I have referred, if at any time there is any reason why you would need to take a break please indicate it to the Trial Chamber and we would of course accommodate with you. And with that I would invite Mr. Hannis to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness ST-215, let me ask you a few additional background questions and I think I can do this in open session. Can you tell us where you lived in 1990 through 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: From 1990 to 1992 I resided in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to the formation of the national or the multi-party system in the former Bosnia, were you a member of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Once the multi-party system was established, did you become the member of some other political party; and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I became a member of the SDS. That's the only party I became a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if we could go into private session for the next couple of questions, I'm asking something that's more specifically identifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, as a member of the SDS in your municipality, were you aware of certain instructions issued in late December 1991 for the organisation and activities of the Serb people in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes. At the group of Serbian members of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the Main Board of the party, we were aware of certain guide-lines given to the representatives of the Serbian people and told them what activities to undertake in view of the crisis that had struck Bosnia and Herzegovina and in view of the events that preceded the breakup of the former Yugoslavia and in view of the events that preceded the breakup of the system of power in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we bring up on the screen Exhibit P15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, in a moment I hope you'll be seeing on your screen a document that we've been talking about. This is the cover page. I think you looked at this during proofing. Do you need to see the inside contents?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Well, if that's not a problem, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this first page we see a reference to Variant A. Do you recall there being two Variants, A and B, for these instructions?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, Variant A was for municipalities where there was a majority population of Serbs; and Variant B was for those where Serbs were in a minority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we have in this case an adjudicated fact, 1372, which indicates that at the time Zvornik was approximately 59 per cent Muslim and 38 per cent Serb. So Zvornik would have been a Variant A municipality under these instructions?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No, Zvornik would be under B because Serbs were a minority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. I misspoke. I meant to say "B." Thank you. And do you recall having these instructions received in Zvornik in late December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I cannot confirm the authenticity of this particular document, but I remember that we received similar guide-lines in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to the documents being received in Zvornik, had you attended any meeting or been present where there were discussions about these instructions prior to them actually being issued?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can't recall being part of the work of a forum that might have prepared these guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't recall being at any meeting of the Deputies' Club where Mr. Krajisnik, Karadzic, Plavsic, and Koljevic discussed the instruction?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: We had a lot of meetings of our Deputies' Club before the conflicts broke out. At many meetings those things were indeed discussed, but your first question was whether I participated in meetings where these things were prepared. I said that I didn't; however, I did attend meetings where there were discussions about the implementation of measures that would ensue after all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you recall when and how the SDS in Zvornik received these instructions from the Main Board? Were they picked up by somebody from Zvornik? Were they faxed or mailed to you, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I really can't remember. A lot of documents arrived at the time. I really can't remember how this particular document arrived, but I've already told you -- I've explained how documents arrived, by mail, by fax, they were brought personally by people from various sessions and meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And once the instructions were received in Zvornik, did the SDS in Zvornik go about implementing the Variant B instructions?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we next take a look at Exhibit P436.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is tab 3. Now, witness, you should see on your screen a document dated the 22nd of December, 1991, called "Conclusions of the SDS ... Municipal Board Meeting ..." and item number 3 shows the election of a Crisis Staff. Do you recall this meeting and this -- these conclusions, including the election of a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the specific meeting or what transpired at that particular meeting, but it is certainly not in dispute that a Crisis Staff was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was the commander Branko Grujic, as is reflected here?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us if any member of the Crisis Staff was also a member of the police and tell us the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Dragan Spasojevic represented the Serbian people in the MUP. He was a commander there -- actually, the commander of the police station in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A couple other names. Can you tell us who Stevo Ivanovic was, what organ was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Stevo Ivanovic was the secretary for national defence in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Kosta Eric?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Kosta Eric worked in the Territorial Defence and he was in charge for civilian protection there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 4 says that: "Jovo Ivanovic is elected co-ordinator for negotiations with the SDA ..." What kinds of negotiations were contemplated with the SDA at that time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Negotiations to deal with all disputable issues and also to prevent any possible incidents. He was appointed as a person who can rally other people around himself in order to talk to the representatives of the Muslim people and deal with any possible problems that had arisen during the inter-ethnic conflict. I don't know how I should put it. I'm talking about developments that were aberrations from any kind of normal behaviour, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could help me with a couple of acronyms. In item number 5 it says: "Any political negotiations with SDA are forbidden to members of GO," it says in my translation, "and MO, except for the people who are authorised to do so by GO." Do you know what those acronyms stand for?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: GO is -- stands for Executive Board, whereas MO stands for local boards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that would be boards of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes, of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to jump forward a bit to --

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to dwell on this document for a while. When I spoke to you I said that the Crisis Staff didn't comprise only SDS members. There were also members who were not SDS members or they were members of another party, and there were people who only subsequently joined the SDS. In other words, there weren't only SDS members in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us which of these named people were not in December 1991 members of the SDS to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Slavoljub Tomasevic, for example, was a member of another party. It was the party of Dudakovic [as interpreted] or whatever his name was. They were the heirs of the communist party and at the time -- Vaso Eric at the time wasn't an SDS member, the same goes for Radislav Peric. Well, these are some of the people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. There is a -- I think small error in line 20 -- it's page 21, line 2. I think it was not Dudakovic, maybe witness said the other name and maybe that was kind of -- that was kind of party, and maybe we could get from the witness what the ethnicity was the president of that party former -- just for the sake of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Witness, and can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The president of the party was a Muslim by ethnicity at the time. I said Dudakovic but I made a mistake. His name wasn't Dudakovic, but perhaps somebody from the Defence remembers the name of the president of the party that followed in the footsteps of the communist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber allows, we can assist, but we can deal with the matter on the cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's only about one letter in the last name of the person in question, one letter should be altered, but it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't see this as being a matter of controversy; it's a matter of historical record. So if the clarification could be made at this point, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of that party was called Durakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Durakovic. I apologise. I made the mistake. The difference really is only one letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nevertheless, these individuals named as members of the Crisis Staff in this document were all Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to go forward to April of 1992 and show you a document that is P323. Now, at the beginning of April were you aware of or did you hear about a take-over facilitated in part by Arkan's men or Arkan's Tigers in Bijeljina municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: We followed the events in Bijeljina on television or on the radio and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see Mrs. Plavsic greeting Arkan in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I saw that in Bijeljina not only Mrs. Plavsic but also a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; in respect of the Muslim people, Fikret Abdic welcomed Arkan in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Take a look at the exhibit that's on the screen, P323 in evidence. It's entitled: "Decision on the Declaration of the State of War on the Territory of the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik." Dated 6th of April, 1992. Were you aware of this decision at the time it was made?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I do not have the paper here. Perhaps this page should be moved. Could this be --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist, we only see the English version on the screen, whereas the other -- oh, now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it needs to be magnified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we need the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can see it. Yes, this is the document that was adopted by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know how it came to be adopted on that date? Was it pursuant to some instruction from higher up or was it simply a decision of the local Crisis Staff of which Mr. Grujic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: This was a decision of the local Crisis Staff, because at that time - and that's the beginning of the conflict in Zvornik - chaos spread and events occurred over which we had no control. And this is an attempt of ours to establish control over the circumstances, that's -- that was our line of thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a particular event that had taken place that led to this decision being adopted or was it the totality of circumstances throughout the municipality and Bosnia, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I'd sooner say that it was a totality of circumstances, but particularly the circumstances in Zvornik; but the situation in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina anywhere was extremely serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Up to this time, though, January through the very beginning of April, in Zvornik municipality were the joint organs working between Muslims and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Up until April 1992 the municipality of Zvornik functioned officially. Until April 1992 there was no official breakup of the municipality, it functioned officially. But the functioning of the municipality was much more difficult. It existed only on paper, whereas from the functional point of view it was practically non-existent. Even then we were completely divided and that happened before April, because there had been a series of incidents which led to a sharp rise of tensions. And there was no point in doing anything. There were many attempts to reach agreement to improve the situation, but Zvornik municipality could not set up control over things. And I can give you examples. There was a murder of a taxi-driver in Zvornik which gave rise to great tensions, and immediately before the conflict there was that attack on a sergeant and a group of soldiers. And then there was distrust and dissent within the MUP, that is, the police. And then there was disagreement and dissent within various municipal services.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question: By geography - I'm no expert on the constitutional law of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina or the RS. I think by education and training you aren't either, but where does a Crisis Staff draw the authority to declare a state of war? Isn't that something that is more left to the National Assembly or the Presidency rather than a local Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Before that event in Zvornik certain decisions were adopted at the level of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. An Assembly or parliament of the RS was established and so was an interim government or a council of ministers. The situation was monitored and there were negotiations with the Muslim side about a peaceful solution to the problem of the breakup of former Yugoslavia and about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You will know that the Cutileiro Plan was signed which envisaged a peaceful break-away of Bosnia-Herzegovina from former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: -- the central authorities were crumbling --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- I don't think you're answering my question. Do you know what authority a Crisis Staff, a municipality Crisis Staff, had under the constitution or any laws in the former Bosnia or in the nascent entity that became the Republika Srpska to declare a state of war, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff declared the state of war in the territory of the Serb municipality of Zvornik. Can you see the title or the heading, that is the Serb municipality of Zvornik, in the area inhabited by Serbs. And when we established a Serb municipality of Zvornik, it -- we did so with the following intention: If there should be a crisis it should take care of the population, it should prevent the escalation of conflicts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- sort of treat that question. Mr. Witness, do I understand your answer to Mr. Hannis's question to be that for purely practical, organisational reasons this is -- this declaration of a state of war was something that was permissible or acceptable at the local level? Do I understand that to be the effect of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From a legal point of view, as the Prosecutor said, or from the constitutional point of view, at the level of the republic that may not have been strictly legal. But with a view to the situation, we constantly speak about law from this vantage point. But I have come here to speak about the situation as it was there and then. Chaos reigned. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had broken apart. There were no authorities, no functioning authorities, and then the Crisis Staff took a decision. Of course it derives its authority merely from the fact that it was established and it tried to create a situation that would lead to normalisation. There was chaos. We couldn't sit there and think about what was lawful and what was not. I hope I have made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, before I go on to the next days in April, let me ask you about the two accused in this case. Did you know Stojan Zupljanin in 1992; and if so, when and how did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I'm certain I didn't know Stojan Zupljanin until after September 1992. I'm sure of that. It must have been after September 1992. When exactly, however, I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you met him after that, what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I met him at the Bosna Hotel in Banja Luka. He was introduced to me by the vice-speaker of the Assembly, Mr. Branko Simic. He introduced him as the security advisor or something like that, Stojan Zupljanin. We were sitting there and talking about unrelated things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it you then had no substantive dealings with him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about Mico Stanisic, can you tell us when and how you first met him and the nature of your contacts with him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not I saw him at a meeting or another in Sarajevo, but I didn't know him personally and we never met personally until the meeting at Sekovici. And that would have been by the end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll talk more about that in a little bit. Let me return to the 6th of April and the declaration of war in Zvornik, Serbian municipality of Zvornik. Do you recall -- I think my calendar shows that the 6th of April was a Monday. Can you tell us how --

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- your day began and what happened the next few days.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day, Brano Grujic came to the building where I was to fetch me. It was early in the morning and I was supposed to go to the factory. He told me that something terrible was happening, that there was conflict, that there were many roadblocks, and that we should urgently go to Celopek where we should all assemble and see what should be done and we should also collect information. We went to Glinica, but we were stopped at a roadblock at Meterize and we were sent back. And then we crossed the Old Bridge to Serbia and then went to the new bridge and crossed to Karakaj. After that we went to Celopek and we tried to establish contact with the members of the Crisis Staff, with Jovo Ivanovic, Stevo Ivanovic, Radic, and the others. Once we succeeded in doing that, we decided that we should move closer to the road, and we decided to go to Alhos, that was a factory that didn't work at the time, and we wanted to collect information about what was going on. That was a moment when you could hear shooting including artillery fire and also small arms fire. All traffic was interrupted and the phones weren't working. We met at Alhos. Once the Crisis Staff was assembled, we decided to go to Alhos. If you want me to continue, I can tell you what happened in the following day --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I interrupt for a minute just to ask you about Alhos. You said it was a factory that didn't work anymore, but where was it located? Was that in the area that's referred to as Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Karakaj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: At Karakaj we tried to collect information about what was going on, where -- how the conflict began, who was fighting who, but we had little success. We couldn't reach any of the officers who were out there with their units, Obrenovic, and at Celopek there was a battalion that had come back from Croatia. I'm not sure of the name. They were involved in the fighting towards Sapna and Zivinice and so on. All that day it was like that until the meeting of the Crisis Staff. After the meeting those volunteers started arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. You mentioned trying to reach some of the officers with their units and you mentioned an Obrenovic. Was that Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he was a captain in the JNA, if I recall correctly?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then you mentioned that there was a meeting of the Crisis Staff. At what time of day on April 6th, if you remember, was that in the afternoon or the evening?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: In the early evening hours or in the late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one or two more questions before we take the first break. You said that after the Crisis Staff meeting those volunteers started arriving. And can you tell us what you mean by "those volunteers." Who were they and where were they from?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: They were Arkan's men. Peja's with Marko Pavlovic arrived, and in front of the building I cannot give the exact number, but there may have been about a dozen of those people. I don't know the exact number, but certainly a group arrived and could be seen outside that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me break it down into a couple more questions. Who was the leader of Arkan's men that came to Alhos on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The leader of the men was Peja. They called him Major Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Marko Pavlovic, who was he? Had you met him before and what did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I saw him after the establishment of the Serb municipality of Zvornik. He was introduced to me by Dragan Spasojevic, who said that he was a Serb businessman who wanted to invest in Zvornik municipality, who wanted to help, and so on. I knew him as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps that's an appropriate time for our first break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so we take the adjournment -- we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, when we broke we were talking about April 6th and Alhos and some of the people who arrived there. You mentioned Marko Pavlovic, who was introduced to you by Dragan Spasojevic, as being a Serb businessman. Later in 1992 or even after the war, did you learn more information about who Marko Pavlovic actually was?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: After the war I found out that Marko Pavlovic was among us under an assumed name, that he had actually come from Sremska Mitrovica or some place; however, I'm not sure that he was born there. And I supposed that he was a member of some federal security service. I'm not sure what exactly the name of that agency would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also on the 6th of April, were any Serbian members of the Zvornik police station arriving at Alhos, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Now I cannot remember whether it was Monday or Tuesday, but I believe that a group arrived on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened the next day, Tuesday, the 7th, did the Crisis Staff meet again?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: On the following day the Crisis Staff met again. They were assembled constantly, as it were, at least most of the members of the Crisis Staff. They were considering what to do and what steps to take. Some information had trickled through about what kind of conflict was going on, where the roadblocks were, what was going on in town, and so on. So we held meetings to see what to do in the future, how -- where we should go from there. One of the suggestions was to set up contact with the president of the municipality, that is the representatives of the Muslims, to negotiate with them and try to solve the situation to learn how they felt about it and what kind of solution could be arrived at.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the name of the president, the Muslim president, of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: His name was Abdulah Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at this Crisis Staff meeting on Tuesday, the 7th of April, were there any outsiders or non-members of the Crisis Staff attending the meeting ?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: When we decided to re-start negotiations with the Muslims, Marko and Peja attended the session of the Crisis Staff. I then had a clash with the so-called Major Peja, and I asked Brano who this man was and why he had come because he was walking about all the time shouting things such as, "What are you doing sitting here and we're -- while people are dying out there?" And then I suggested that he leave, and so he did, angrily. I suggested --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Marko you refer to is Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I suggested and we decided to re-start negotiations with the Muslims. I said that I had a clash with Peja and Marko Pavlovic was at the meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what was done about the decision to try and negotiate with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Later Jovo Ivanovic called up Pasic and they spoke to see where we could meet and decide what to do later. We were not sure that we could guarantee him security on our side and he wasn't sure that he could guarantee our security in Zvornik, so it was Pasic who suggested that we meet at Mali Zvornik in Serbia and we accepted. And we went there on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you went to Mali Zvornik on Wednesday, the 8th, also on Tuesday, the same day that you decided to try and have some further negotiations, did the Crisis Staff take any decision about mobilising any forces in light of the crisis?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did take decisions once the state of war was declared, including a mobilisation order. I don't remember the exact date, but we tried to mobilise people to raise the reserve forces and established some units and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us what happened the next day, Wednesday, 8 April.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: On the following day, Jovo Ivanovic and I went to that meeting. Stevo Ivanovic was supposed to come along but didn't. So the two of us went. We were driven there by one of the journalists who was there and he had a car and he offered us to take us to Mali Zvornik. We went to the Jezera Hotel with him, that's at Mali Zvornik, and we met Pasic there and Alija Kapidzic who was commander of the TO for Zvornik. They were the Muslim representatives. We sat down to talk -- actually, we had coffee and then when we wanted to start talking we asked the journalists to leave and that we would give a statement to him later and he got up and left. We asked the hotel personnel to find us a room where we would be undisturbed. He left to look for a room, and during that time we spoke to them. And even now I remember that they told us what the situation was like in Zvornik where a Muslim population was left behind and where they were too. I remember perfectly that they said that the situation was almost the same as it was on our side, that there was utter chaos, that there were many new people whom they didn't know, that they were setting up check-points all over the place, they were stopping people, searching for weapons, even searching houses and homes. That's what the two of us told us while we were still there sitting there with nobody else present. After that short conversation, the head waiter arrived, but with him there were armed people and they ordered us to follow them. They took us to the Municipal Assembly of Mali Zvornik. We were taken into a large room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I stop you there just to clarify. Mali Zvornik is across the river in Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: In Serbia, yes, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these armed men who took you to the room, what do you know about them or what did you later learn about who they were?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about them. I didn't know then, I don't know now, but I'm sure that they were Arkan's men. They were his men because the uniforms that they wore were not uniforms either of the army or the police. Shall I continue or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Please tell us what happened when you arrived in this large room.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: When we arrived in this large room, in the central part there was Arkan standing there. That was the first time I saw him in person. I'd not seen him before, but I knew him from television and from newspapers and so on. And there were a lot of people standing around him. We were brought in and they asked us who we were. I said, "I'm a deputy and this is the president of the Executive Board, the president of the municipality of Zvornik," and so on and so forth. And then he said, "What are you doing here?" And I said, "We are negotiating." "What about?" And now I have to go back to something I forgot to say. Before we set off when Jovo Ivanovic had spoken to Pasic, Pasic told him this, "We are ready and we accept to divide the municipality into a Muslim part and a Serbian part to keep peace and to keep good relations." That's what we had in mind and that's what we wanted to do. Then Arkan said, "Take the two outside and the traitors should remain here." And then he said, "What are you doing here? Why are you doing?" "We are negotiating." "What about?" "We are negotiating about the division of the municipality and restoring peace." And he says, "Who authorised you to do that, traitors? This is not your job. You have to defend the Serbian people. The Serbs are dying out there and you are negotiating with Muslims. Zvornik is just one municipality and it's an integral municipality and it cannot be split with the Muslims." I had never heard that before. And then Peja approached us and hit both me and Jovo Ivanovic. And when that was over he said, "Take them out." We found ourselves in front of the municipality building and we were waiting for a car to take us across the river. While we were there waiting, Marko Pavlovic got out and he said, "I'll give you a lift back." En route to Alhos Marko Pavlovic told us this, "And now, lads, your political days are over. Go back to your companies. This is not the work for you." And as of that moment onwards, we really no longer engaged in politics. We both returned to our respective companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few more specific questions about this event. In addition to Arkan in this large room, do you remember anybody else present in the room when this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: In addition to Arkan, I remember that there were two guys named Jekic and one of them was Vojo Jekic. In my opinion, he probably had a lot to do with the events. He was quite influential. I saw him in Zvornik on a few occasions. There was also Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer; Dragan Obrenovic; there was Marko Pavlovic; there was also the secretary for the police from Mali Zvornik; and a few other men whom I can't remember as I sit here today. In any case there were a lot of people there, Peja and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the conversation when Arkan said, "Take those two out and keep the traitors here," the two that were taken out were the Muslims, Mr. Pasic and Mr. Kapidzic?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say Peja hit you and Mr. Ivanovic. How was that? Was that a slap? Was that one punch? Was it multiple blows? How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I must admit that Ivanovic received more blows than I did. I was slapped twice or three times and kicked twice or three times, and he was slapped many more times than I was and also kicked many more times than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So on the 8th Pavlovic took you back to where, Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: To Karakaj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened then on the 8th in Zvornik town, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I don't know exactly at what point in time, but later on I heard that Arkan had given an ultimatum to Kapidzic and Pasic for weapons to be surrendered by either 1.00 or 2.00, and he told them that he knew exactly how many rifles they had. That's what I heard. And then he let them go. I heard that he had not ill-treated them or beaten them. At that point that same evening or perhaps in the afternoon, later in the afternoon, Zvornik came under attack. I don't know exactly. I was in the factory, I wasn't there, but I believe that the attack against Zvornik started sometime in the afternoon that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what forces on the Serb side were involved in that attack and eventual take-over of the town? Was it army? Police? Civilians? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I cannot be a reliable witness to that. I can only tell you what I heard. The central figure of all those developments was Arkan. I don't know if there were any other paramilitaries in addition to Arkan. I don't know who else was involved, whether any members of the military were involved. I don't know. I can't confirm because I didn't see any of that. I don't know. I wasn't present while that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We have adjudicated facts about that. Let me ask you about the next Crisis Staff meeting after the 8th of April. Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The next Crisis Staff meeting was on the following day, on Thursday. Jovan Ivanovic and I were again invited to attend the meeting. The Crisis Staff meeting was called in order to set up some sort of power that could be in power; that was the explanation. And the explanation was that there were no authorities on either of the sides, at least not any functioning authorities. Marko Pavlovic's proposal was to set up an interim government, and the Crisis Staff concluded that this interim government should indeed be set up, that the existing bodies of government should be disbanded, and that new authorities should be set up. And I don't know, it wasn't actually said precisely how that would be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have some documents that purport to be from the provisional government or temporary government as it's sometimes translated. Do you know why this provisional government was created instead of just continuing with the Crisis Staff and do you know whose idea was it? I guess anyone other than Marko Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can't tell you whose idea that was. I can only speculate. However, I heard that it was Marko Pavlovic's proposal, that he was the one who was of the opinion that this provisional or temporary government should be set up. I don't know whether he discussed it with somebody else. I can't tell you because I never attended any such discussions or meetings if there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, from the documents it appears the provisional government was set up sometime around the 9th or 10th of April and continued to function until sometime in late August. During that time did you attend any sessions of the provisional government?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I was asked by my managing director in my company to attend any meetings when economic issues and mobilisation issues were on the agenda. He asked me to protect people from the Glinica company. The Glinica company was an important company, and when the number of staff was down we experienced a lot of technical problems, we couldn't function properly, and that's how I came to attend some of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where you were and what you were doing during the approximately ten days to two weeks between April 8th and April 20th of 1992, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I was in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was the first time after the conflict started that you returned to Zvornik town itself?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I believe that I returned to Zvornik around the 20th of April, but I can't swear to that. I believe it was around the 20th of April that I went back to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us what did you see when you went into Zvornik town, what were you able to observe about the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that there was a lot of debris and rubble in Zvornik. All the streets were in a state of disarray. Many shop windows were broken. I could see a lot of armed people roaming the streets, and on some shop windows there were inscriptions. When I arrived at my building my apartment was in a good state of order, nobody had touched it, but all of the Muslim apartments in my building had been broken into, and I'm talking about my building only and the apartments that had been broken in in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your building approximately how many flats were there?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Approximately 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And of those 80, what was the division between Serb-owned and Muslim-owned properties?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a couple of documents from the provisional government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could first show the witness 65 ter 2605. And we need to enlarge the left-hand page of the B/C/S I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is in my English translation entitled: "A Decision to Form the Territorial Defence Command ..." dated the 28th of April, listing Marko Pavlovic as commander. Do you remember when this decision was passed?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was Branko Grujic the head or president of the interim government at that time?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: He was the president of the interim government from the 9th of April onwards. That's from the day the government was set up until the moment the municipality Assembly had been reinstated to its previous status.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why Marko Pavlovic, this outsider, had been appointed head of the TO in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can say that I don't know who he had spoken to and about what. It would be speculation if I told you anything. However, I can tell you that at that time on day one and day two after the exit from Zvornik it was a problem to find a person who would lead the Territorial Defence. To put it simply, there was simply no people. I remember that one guy was appointed and left the position on -- within the scope of one day. I don't know why Marko Pavlovic was appointed. I can't tell you that I am a reliable witness to that. If I told you anything, it would be mere speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the nature of the relationship between Mr. Grujic and Mr. Pavlovic in terms of their working together?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Their relationship, it was fair based on what anybody could observe. They didn't have any mutual conflicts. They co-operated normally, they socialised normally, but in terms of their relationship and how they functioned I don't know. But from what one could observe I would say that their relationship was fair, that they were fair to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was certainly better than your relationship with Major Peja?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I did not have any relationship with Major Peja after the events in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more, Witness, from the provisional government. This is tab 13. It's 65 ter 2607.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think we need the right-hand page enlarged of the B/C/S. No, I'm sorry. I've got the wrong page. Could I see the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a decision dated the -- also the 28th of April, and it's -- at the top says: "Following Article 5 of the decision on the declaration of the state of war ..." This is a decision relating to a commission for cleaning up the battle-field. Item III says: "Cleaning up of battle-field duties shall be transferred to the TO staff command of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik." Before this date, do you know whose responsibility it was in the municipality for cleanup of battle-fields, what department or section?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The department in charge of that before the war was the department for civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why this change was made, to transfer those duties to the Territorial Defence command?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know why that was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 2607.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1606, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, after the take-over of Zvornik town did you observe or hear what was happening in Muslim villages outside the town in Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: After the take-over of Zvornik municipality, many Muslim villages were torched. Muslims in the villages -- I can't remember the name -- oh, right, Djulici, Kozluk, and Sepak were cut off from the Drina River because the front line was slowly moving towards Zivinice and Tuzla, and Muslims from the upper part of the Drina Valley, they withdrew towards Vlasenica and there was a front line set up in the direction of Vlasenica. That was the situation around that time, and those people who remained in Djulici, Kozluk, and Sepak were in extremely dire straits. They didn't work, they didn't have electricity, they didn't have water, they didn't have food. Nobody helped them. Nobody guaranteed their safety. They were exposed to the paramilitaries who stormed in, arrested people, intercepted vehicles, set up check-points. Their situation in a nutshell was not enviable at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with those Muslim villages that were being torched, what was happening with the Muslim villagers who lived there? Did you hear about arrests and killings of some of those people?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: A majority of the villagers left the area of Zvornik and a lot of those did indeed manage to leave it; however, the gangs that stormed the villages, if they happened to come across somebody -- I heard that there had been cases -- if they came across somebody they were known to kill those people on the spot. And they also arrested some people and took them to the prisons that they'd themselves had set up in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know the names and locations of any of those prisons set up in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: In Zvornik places where Muslims were incarcerated were at Divice, in Celopek, at the farm. I can't give you any more details. I can't give you any more places, but most times those three were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally tell anybody in the government or any other authorities about these crimes, these killings and torchings of villages, the arrest and detention in those prisons?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The first contacts I had after the events in Mali Zvornik was with the MP Micic from Bijeljina. He was the first one who heard from me what had happened to me and how the power changed hands in Zvornik. And the first occasion I had to talk to somebody at the higher level was a meeting in Sekovici. That was my first direct contact with somebody representing the republican government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you go further on that let me ask you one question about Mr. Micic from Bijeljina. Do you recall his first name?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Dragan Micic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall approximately when you had that first conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. However, it was at one of the meetings of the regional board in Ugljevik. I had been invited to the meeting and I saw him there. Since I had not attended the first Assembly meeting at the time I was cut off from the rest of the world. That was my first occasion to see him and that's when I shared with him the detail of that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall having taken part in an interview with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, Stephen Margetts and Brett Simpson in June 2002 when you gave a written statement?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in terms of when you may have spoken to Mr. Micic, do you recall having indicated that that would have been sometime before the Assembly session on the 12th of May in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You weren't able to attend that session because of the travel difficulties to get from Zvornik to Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I didn't even know that there would be such a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about the meeting in Sekovici. Where is Sekovici? Is that a town? Is that a municipality? Where is it vis-a-vis Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Sekovici is a municipality which borders on Zvornik. It's between Zvornik, Vlasenica, and Kalesija, that's where it's located.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the nature of this meeting that you attended? Do you know who had called the meeting and for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Brano Grujic invited me to Glinica. He told me that people from the government of the republic are coming and that they wanted to see the members of the Municipal Assembly and the members of the Executive Board and so on. They wanted all those people to come to Sekovici to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately how many people did attend?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can't exactly remember how many, but there were all sort of people. There were members of the Assembly, members of the Executive Board, presidents of municipalities, members of Municipal Boards of the SDS. I don't know whether there were representatives of the army and the police. I can't remember any individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there as many as 50?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I don't think so. Not as many as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: More than 20?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Let's say around 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And who were the representatives from the republican government who were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The authorities of the republic were represented by Mico Stanisic and Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the topic of discussion?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: It was that people on the ground be informed that a government of the republic was being established and that on behalf of their ministries they should say what the current situation is like and what plans were in place for the future. And they also wanted to hear about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you speak or provide any information to Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic about the situation in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I did take the floor at the meeting, but I very briefly merely said what had happened with regard to Arkan and much along the lines of the words of other people, that there were paramilitaries in Zvornik and that they were acting on their own, stopping people, searching them, looting, killing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what reaction or response was there from those two, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: They informed us that the ministries were being established and that they had no funds. They were trying to set up a ministry on a greenfield as it were, that they didn't have personnel or any ways of assisting the municipalities financially or in terms of resources. But they gave instructions that attempts should be made to -- for the police not to be involved in combat activities and that efforts shall be made to provide security, that it should be the police to control the situation on the ground to the extent possible rather than the TO or the army. They said that they couldn't integrate the entire system now, but that they would strive to achieve that for network to be put in place so that everybody be able to establish contact with the central authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Mr. Mandic was at that time associated with the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can't remember now who spoke on behalf of which ministry, but they said that they were there as representatives of the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice respectively. But who was who, I don't know now. I think that Mandic represented the Ministry of Justice, whereas Mico spoke for the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall telling Mr. Margetts and Mr. Simpson in 2002, paragraph 132 of your statement: "I think that Momcilo Mandic attended the meeting in Sekovici as a representative of the Ministry of the Interior"?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Well, no. I'm saying even now I think. I'm not sure. I cannot state with certainty that I remember how they introduced themselves. Why am I saying now that I think it was different? Let me explain. I had the opportunity to see a document about the election of the Council of Ministers so that for that reason I think that what I said is more likely than the alternative, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You think your memory is better today than it was in 2002 about the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I saw a document about the appointment of that interim -- or what was it called? The Council of Ministers actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but are you talking about a document related to the Assembly of the Serb people in BiH?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the document I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is it about that document that leads you to believe that Momcilo Mandic was associated with the Ministry of Justice at the time of this meeting in Sekovici? I don't understand the connection between those two things.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you I wasn't sure. But when I saw that document the idea came to me that it could be that way, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what is it about that document that makes you think that? Was Mr. Mandic's name on it?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No. There is a document for the Assembly that speaks about Mico Stanisic being a candidate for the position of minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you're not aware of Momcilo Mandic serving for a time as the deputy minister of the interior in the beginning weeks of the war, April/early May 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of the date of the meeting in Sekovici in your statement in 2002 you indicated it was a few weeks after the start of the war. Is that still -- was that still your memory?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we've heard a lot of evidence about some of the actions by various paramilitary groups in Zvornik including the Yellow Wasps, but before I get to that besides speaking to Mr. Micic and Mr. Stanisic and Mandic at the Sekovici meeting, did you inform any other people in the government, any of the higher authorities, about these crimes that you were aware of in April and May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I don't know when my first contact with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik was. It was at Pale on the occasion of an Assembly meeting, but I didn't have the chance to speak to either for any -- for a longer period because Karadzic left the meeting and Krajisnik didn't have much time. But I spoke to the vice-president of the Assembly, Branko Simic, who promised me that he would relate everything I had said to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's talk about the Muslims leaving Zvornik municipality in 1992. I think in your statement you mentioned that you were involved I think on four occasions with negotiations with some of those groups who wanted to leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: In talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the first occasion -- I'm sorry. Can you tell us about the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: First it was about the return of people who were preparing to leave Kozluk. Two soldiers came to Glinica to fetch me. They were saying that Major Peja wanted to see me and Ivanovic at Kozluk to try to persuade the people not to leave. Ivanovic wasn't there but I was, so I went to Kozluk. The people had really gathered to leave Kozluk. They were all on tractor-trailers, on trucks, cars with all their belongings, et cetera. They were setting off. I spoke to a mufti and a bishop, and they wanted to speak out, to address the people. They climbed on a tractor-trailer and were saying to the people that they shouldn't leave, that the situation would calm down, et cetera, but they couldn't make any specific promises. They couldn't promise them any things. I didn't speak then. Later there was an occasion when the people from Kozluk asked questions about how security can be provided for them and how the situation could be changed. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Djulici, did you get involved in discussions or negotiations about the Muslims from Djulici leaving Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Should I continue or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The Muslims from Djulici requested somebody to come and talk to them and they did so for quite a time. They asked to see people who could provide them guarantees and -- so that they could feel safe and so that they could decide what they should do. They had met Peja and Marko and Brano Grujic, that's what they said to us when we went there to see them; and some of them, our people from that area, told me that they wanted to see somebody who is not in the structures of authority because they didn't believe that they were getting complete information. We met one day and agreed to go and see those people so that I, Dragan Spasojevic, Vinko Radovic, Nikola Spasojevic, and there was another man from that area -- anyway, there was a group of some seven, eight people. But before we left we saw Branko Grujic and Pavlovic. We asked them what was happening to those people and what the problem was up there, and then we learned that they had spoken to them and that they had told them they couldn't solve their problems, that they didn't have any personnel to guard them, and so on. The -- but if they felt unsafe they were free to leave. If they want to leave, they were free to do so but only to Serbia and by no means toward the front line. They could take their personal belongings and everybody was free to leave. But that was -- wasn't to be understood as an order to those people but only in case they want to leave that was the way to go about it. When we arrived at Djulici at the house of Vinko Radovic, three or four Muslims arrived and there was about a dozen of us and we listened to the people describing the situation they were in and what was going on there. They told us that before the war there were about 7.000 of them, whereas now only 2500 had remained. They didn't have any work, no food, all shops were closed, there was no medication available, and that they were in dire straits. And they were looking for a solution. They asked whether anybody could provide security for them, but the answer to that was negative. And we said that we also heard that there were no forces available to provide security. They were saying that daily there were raids, that there were some men searching houses and people, arresting people, and so on. They said that they were rough and ready to go and they were inquiring as to how they could leave, and we told them what Branko Grujic's and Marko Pavlovic's message to them was. And they accepted that as the only option.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand it the message was they could leave but they could only go to Serbia, they could only take their hand luggage with them, and buses would be provided for them to leave; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did that happen? Were the people from Djulici allowed to leave in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I wasn't in Zvornik when the people left Djulici, but I can say that according to what I heard from the people who were there when they left that something terrible happened. Marko Pavlovic separated or singled out a certain number of men from the others. They sent off the rest of them to Serbia, whereas these men were detained at the technical school in Zvornik. They were locked up there at the school and they were guarded by the TO. When I first saw Marko Pavlovic I asked him why he had done that and how he could have done that, since he had been promising to the people that they could leave. And he replied that in Tuzla there were a large number of soldiers who had been taken prisoner. He wasn't -- I'm not sure of the number he mentioned. And he said, "I have a list and now we can exchange one group for the other." And I said that that wasn't right and it wasn't in line with the promises made to those people and that was no way to treat people because they weren't soldiers but civilians, and he angrily replied that it wasn't for me to tell the TO what to do. And that's how our conversation about that ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know and did you hear what happened to those men from Djulici who had been separated out and detained at the technical school -- is that Karakaj technical school?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: Karakaj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear what happened to those men? Were they exchanged or what?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: According to what I heard, they were not exchanged. There was talk by the people from the TO who were securing the place that starting from the first day of their detention every night soldiers of Repic and Zuco or that paramilitary from Nis, Pivarski, maltreated them nightly and took some of them away and that many people came to harm that way. Marko Pavlovic, probably in a desire to stop that, organised their passage to Serbia. They tried to -- correction, he tried to take them to Serbia, but it would seem that the paramilitaries got the better of him because the on the way there many people got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you, after learning this about what Marko Pavlovic had done with the men from Djulici, did you report that to anybody in the higher authorities in the RS?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: On the first opportunity I had, I spoke to Branko Simic about that, and on one occasion I even spoke to Karadzic and Krajisnik about that. And I told him in rough terms what had happened to those people according to what I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the reaction from those three, if any?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The reaction -- their reaction was - how should I put it? - it met with great disapproval and they couldn't believe themselves that things like that could happen. Karadzic himself on several occasions condemned any mistreatment of civilians or separation of civilians or taking hostages, and he even issued orders to that effect. He was very disappointed by what had happened in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, if any action or discipline or criminal charges were ever placed against Marko Pavlovic and his men in connection with those events?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No, except for the fact that now he's standing trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what that's for in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I don't know any details, but I think it's about this event and the overall situation in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the houses that were left behind by departing Muslims? I assume that not all of them were torched. What became of that property, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: The people from Djulici said the following, "Whence we leave we would like our houses to remain intact and unburned, and if possible the authorities should see to it that the houses be preserved." And it was their suggestion for the refugees, of who there were many in Zvornik, to move into their houses so that the houses remain intact, to keep them from torching. Later the transition authorities indeed decided to house refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could show you now Exhibit 65 ter 2614. I think this relates to what you're talking about. It would be the right-hand page I believe. My English describes this as a "decision regarding the seizing of abandoned and uninhibited" - probably means uninhabited - "residential and business premises in the region of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik," dated I think the 12th of May, 1992. Is this the provisional government decision you're talking about to deal with abandoned property?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: As far as I can understand this, this decision is a general decision that doesn't apply to any specific cases. This decision covers all of the territories that had been abandoned in Zvornik municipality, that had been abandoned and that would be abandoned from then onwards. That's how I interpret this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1607, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, during April through September of 1992, did you have any duties? Did you have to do any work service?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I had a work obligation in my company, Glinica, and that was installed immediately. The transitional government started giving me either a military obligation or a work obligation, and as an MP I was assigned a work obligation in the Glinica company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the nature of your work obligation? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: I was affiliated with the department which stored finished products and planned the use of spare parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any duties in conjunction with communications?

utterances.speaker: ST-215
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a minute or two early, but this would be a convenient point for me to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
